scams.name: Hartsfield-Jackson (ATL) Airport Rideshare & Taxi Scams
scams.description: ATL is the world's busiest airport by passenger volume (2019-2023). The legitimate Uber/Lyft ride to downtown Atlanta runs $20–$35 depending on surge; licensed taxi is approximately $30–$45 to downtown with the meter. Scam variants: (1) drivers soliciting at baggage claim offering 'flat $60' to downtown — unlicensed; (2) 'limo' or 'black car' touts quoting $80–$120 for standard-distance trips; (3) Uber/Lyft drivers who accept the ride then insist on additional 'tip' or 'airport surcharge' in cash at drop-off; (4) fake MARTA 'ticket agents' in the airport selling overpriced transit passes. The MARTA train runs from ATL to downtown (Five Points station) for $2.50 — scam-proof, 20 minutes, runs every 10–15 minutes. r/travelchina 'Taxi drivers in China airports and train station' (comments/1ks12o9, 2025) captures the universal airport-taxi rule that applies at ATL equally. For older travelers arriving at ATL, the protective playbook: (1) take MARTA Red or Gold line from the ATL station to downtown: $2.50, 20 min, scam-proof; (2) use Uber or Lyft from the designated rideshare pickup zones (North Terminal: North Economy Parking; South Terminal: South Economy Parking) — screenshot fare estimate; (3) if licensed taxi, ensure meter is running and expect $30–$45 to downtown; (4) never engage drivers soliciting at baggage claim or outside terminal doors; (5) ignore 'MARTA ticket agents' — buy Breeze Card at the official MARTA station kiosk for $2.50.
scams.avoidance: MARTA Red/Gold Line from ATL to Five Points downtown: $2.50, 20 min Uber/Lyft at designated rideshare pickup (North or South Terminal Economy Parking) Licensed taxi with meter running: $30–$45 to downtown Never engage drivers soliciting at baggage claim Buy Breeze Card at official MARTA kiosk for $2.50
scams.location: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) arrivals, North/South Terminal pickup zones, MARTA station

scams.name: Georgia Aquarium & Coca-Cola Museum Reseller Scams
scams.description: Atlanta's three main tourist attractions are clustered at Pemberton Place: Georgia Aquarium, World of Coca-Cola, and CNN Center. Legitimate prices: Georgia Aquarium adult $49.95 via georgiaaquarium.org; World of Coca-Cola adult $22 via worldofcoca-cola.com; CNN Center tours $18 via cnn.com (tour discontinued in 2023 — current offerings vary). Scam variants: (1) third-party reseller websites sell Georgia Aquarium at $75–$120 per person — 50–150% markup; (2) 'CityPASS bundles' at $95 per person — legitimate CityPASS exists at citypass.com ($85-$95 depending on dates) but fake resellers sell similar-looking bundles at inflated rates; (3) touts at Centennial Olympic Park offer 'combo tickets' to Aquarium+Coca-Cola at $120+ vs $72 direct. For older travelers visiting Atlanta, the practical playbook: (1) Georgia Aquarium tickets direct at georgiaaquarium.org — adult $49.95; (2) World of Coca-Cola direct at worldofcoca-cola.com — adult $22; (3) genuine Atlanta CityPASS at citypass.com — $85-$95 for 5 attractions including Georgia Aquarium + World of Coca-Cola + Zoo Atlanta + Fernbank Museum + College Football Hall of Fame, only buy from citypass.com directly; (4) reject touts at Centennial Olympic Park offering 'combo tickets'; (5) avoid Google ads for 'Atlanta Aquarium tickets' — they lead to resellers.
scams.avoidance: Georgia Aquarium direct: georgiaaquarium.org, adult $49.95 World of Coca-Cola direct: worldofcoca-cola.com, adult $22 Atlanta CityPASS direct: citypass.com, $85-$95 for 5 attractions Reject touts at Centennial Olympic Park Avoid Google ads for 'Atlanta tickets' — scroll past sponsored results
scams.location: Online — third-party reseller sites for Georgia Aquarium, World of Coca-Cola, CNN Center tickets; touts at Pemberton Place

scams.name: 'US Customs and Border Protection' Phone Scam
scams.description: A 2025 Atlanta-area phone scam specifically targets international travelers and visitors to Atlanta. r/Scams 'Got a Call from Atlanta's US Customs and Border Protection' (comments/1p1lnfu, 2025) is the named 2025 anchor: 'scammers spoof a 404-area-code phone number, claim to be from US Customs and Border Protection, and tell the victim a 'package containing illegal substances has been seized at Hartsfield-Jackson' addressed to them — they must pay a 'fine' of $1,000–$5,000 via Zelle, gift cards, or wire transfer to 'avoid arrest.' The scam pattern includes: (1) caller ID spoofed to show '(404) xxx-xxxx' Atlanta area code; (2) caller claims to be CBP or Homeland Security officer; (3) demands immediate payment to 'clear the warrant'; (4) threatens arrest at the airport if victim doesn't comply; (5) sometimes transfers the call to another 'supervisor' for added legitimacy. For older travelers (who are disproportionately targeted by this scam), the absolute rules: (1) US Customs and Border Protection NEVER calls travelers demanding payment by phone — all communications are in writing via official USPS mail; (2) CBP never accepts Zelle, Venmo, wire transfer, gift cards, or cryptocurrency for any legitimate payment; (3) hang up immediately on any such call — do not engage, do not confirm your name, do not say 'yes' to anything; (4) report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov or call the FTC at 1-877-382-4357; (5) if you're genuinely concerned, call CBP directly at 1-877-CBP-5511 (CBP's real number, easily verified).
scams.avoidance: Hang up immediately — CBP never calls demanding payment by phone Never confirm your name or say 'yes' to a suspicious caller Report to Federal Trade Commission: reportfraud.ftc.gov Verify by calling CBP directly: 1-877-CBP-5511 (official number) CBP communicates legitimate matters via USPS mail only, never Zelle/gift cards
scams.location: Phone calls to travelers visiting Atlanta or transiting through ATL airport, claiming to be from US Customs/ATL area code (404)

scams.name: MLK Center & Sweet Auburn Tour Touts
scams.description: The Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park (MLK Center, birthplace home, Ebenezer Baptist Church, King Center) is FREE to visit. The birthplace home tour requires a free reservation via the National Park Service (nps.gov/malu). Scam variants: (1) street touts outside the Ebenezer Baptist Church offer '$30 private tour' of the MLK sites — everything is free and self-guided; (2) 'MLK Walking Tour' packages at $80+ per person marketed by third-party operators when the free ranger-led tour is comprehensive; (3) 'Sweet Auburn historic walking tour' bundles at $100+ — the Sweet Auburn district is a free pedestrian heritage zone. For older travelers, the MLK Historical Park is a genuinely moving free experience: (1) reserve birthplace home tour at recreation.gov (free, limited daily spots); (2) MLK Center (the tomb and reflection pool) is always free and accessible; (3) Ebenezer Baptist Church is free (historical site); (4) the King Center across the street is also free; (5) skip all paid 'walking tours' — the NPS ranger-led tours are higher quality and free.
scams.avoidance: Reserve MLK birthplace home tour at recreation.gov (free) MLK Center, Ebenezer Baptist, King Center — all free, walk-in NPS ranger-led tour is free and higher quality than paid tours Sweet Auburn historic district is a free self-guided walk Skip all paid 'MLK walking tours'
scams.location: Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, Sweet Auburn Historic District, Ebenezer Baptist Church approach, King Center tours

scams.name: Ponce City Market & Beltline Tourist-Menu Overcharge
scams.description: Ponce City Market (the former Sears, Roebuck building converted to food hall) is Atlanta's signature food destination. It's a legitimate venue with quality vendors, but some stalls are tourist-priced (e.g., $20+ sandwiches, $18+ hot dogs). The adjacent Atlanta BeltLine's Eastside Trail is lined with restaurants and bars charging 40–60% above residential Atlanta pricing. Buckhead tourist-facing venues (near the Mall at Lenox) similarly inflate for expense-account and tourist traffic. For older travelers, the practical guide: (1) Ponce City Market is worth visiting — but eat at mid-tier vendors with posted prices ($12–$18 per meal): Holeman and Finch, El Super Pan, King of Pops; (2) for authentic Atlanta food at residential pricing, go to Virginia-Highland (The Nook, La Fonda), Grant Park (Grant Central Pizza), or Cabbagetown (Agave); (3) BeltLine Eastside Trail restaurants are drink-tourism venues — $14 cocktails and $18 small plates common; (4) Buckhead tourist venues are high-end expense-account territory, not tourist-friendly value; (5) for Southern soul food, Mary Mac's Tea Room ($18–$28 per person — institutional), Paschal's (Westside, $22–$35), or Busy Bee Cafe (Westside, $15–$22).
scams.avoidance: Ponce City Market mid-tier: Holeman and Finch, El Super Pan, King of Pops ($12–$18) Virginia-Highland or Grant Park for residential-priced Atlanta food Mary Mac's Tea Room ($18–$28), Paschal's ($22–$35), Busy Bee Cafe ($15–$22) for soul food Avoid BeltLine Eastside Trail drink tourism (overpriced) Check Yelp/Google for Atlanta restaurants with 4.5+ stars at residential prices
scams.location: Ponce City Market food hall, Atlanta BeltLine (Eastside Trail) restaurant strips, Buckhead tourist-facing venues

scams.name: Atlanta Airbnb & Convention-Season Short-Term Rental Fraud
scams.description: Atlanta hosts major conventions and events year-round (Dragon Con, Music Midtown, Atlanta Falcons/Hawks games, SEC championships) that create tight lodging markets and fertile ground for short-term rental fraud. The scam: a listing on Airbnb, Facebook Marketplace, or Craigslist advertises a Midtown or Downtown apartment at 30–50% below the convention-week hotel price; the 'host' demands deposit via Zelle, Venmo, or wire transfer; listing is either fraudulent or double-booked with multiple victims for the same dates. The high-risk weeks when Atlanta hotels are scarcest: Dragon Con (late August/early September), Music Midtown (September), Falcons/Hawks home games in fall/winter, SEC Football Championship (December), National Black Arts Festival, and Atlanta Dogwood Festival. For older travelers considering Atlanta accommodation, especially during convention weeks: (1) book only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com with platform-verified payment and cancellation protection; (2) refuse Zelle, Venmo, or bank transfer payment requests from any 'host'; (3) verify listings with 20+ reviews from last 12 months; (4) licensed hotels with posted prices: Four Seasons Atlanta, Ritz-Carlton Atlanta, Loews Atlanta, W Atlanta Midtown, Kimpton Sylvan Hotel — all book via Booking.com or the hotel's own site; (5) during convention season, book 3+ months ahead to avoid the scam-vulnerable last-minute market.
scams.avoidance: Book only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com with platform-verified payment Refuse Zelle/Venmo/bank transfer from 'hosts' Verify listings with 20+ reviews from last 12 months Licensed hotels: Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, Loews, W, Kimpton Sylvan Book 3+ months ahead for convention weeks to avoid scam-vulnerable last-minute market
scams.location: Online — Airbnb listings for Midtown, Downtown, Buckhead during Atlanta convention season (January, March, May, October); Facebook Marketplace short-term rentals
